Neonates of the North African elephant shrew Petrosaltator rozeti emerge from the uterus after a gestation period that is remarkably extended for a mammal of its size. Early estimates cited a gestation of 49 to 56 days, but more recent controlled laboratory data indicate that, under a stable ambient temperature of 33.6 °C [T = 33.6 °C], the true gestation time is approximately 76 days [tg = approximately 76 days]. This extended gestational duration is unusual among small afrotherian insectivores and may be linked to the advanced state of neural development observed in the neonates. At parturition, the newborn pups have a modest wet body mass of just 8.1 grams [Wwb = 8.1 grams], a figure that aligns with the species’ overall energetic economy. Female adults ultimately attain a much larger asymptotic body mass, with the ultimate wet weight in females reaching approximately 63 grams [Wwi = approximately 63 grams], though field records from the Animal Diversity Web indicate a broader range of 25 to 70 grams for adult individuals.

Under the same controlled thermal conditions maintained at 33.6 °C [T = 33.6 °C], the developmental trajectory of the young unfolds according to a precise schedule. The time since birth at weaning, marking the transition to nutritional independence from maternal milk, is recorded at 14 days [tx = 14 days] at a temperature of 33.6 °C [T = 33.6 °C]. At this critical juncture, the juveniles have achieved a wet body mass of 18 grams [Wwx = 18 grams], representing more than a doubling of their birth weight. This rapid mass gain is fueled entirely by the lipid-rich milk provided by the mother, and the weaning process itself appears to be abrupt, with the mother ceasing nursing shortly after this point. The relatively early weaning age is consistent with the pattern seen in other elephant shrew species, which typically produce fast-growing, highly precocial young that are capable of foraging for small invertebrates soon after leaving the nest.

Following weaning, the juvenile period is characterized by continued somatic growth and the acquisition of adult foraging skills. Puberty, defined as the onset of gonadal maturation and the ability to produce viable gametes, occurs relatively early in the life cycle of Petrosaltator rozeti. Under the standard laboratory temperature of 33.6 °C [T = 33.6 °C], the time since birth at puberty has been documented to be 45 days [tp = 45 days]. This value falls within a reported range of 40 to 50 days, indicating some plasticity depending on individual condition and resource availability. The attainment of sexual maturity at such a young age, roughly 6.5 weeks after birth, suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes an early onset of reproductive potential. This is likely an adaptation to fluctuating resource availability in its semi-arid North African habitat, where favorable conditions may be unpredictable but require rapid reproductive output when they occur.

The maximum reproductive rate of Petrosaltator rozeti reflects an opportunistic breeding strategy. Females produce approximately 2 young per litter [N_R_i = approximately 2 young per litter], and field observations indicate that they can raise approximately 2 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 litters per year] under optimal conditions maintained at 33.6 °C [T = 33.6 °C]. This annual reproductive output is relatively modest compared to many small rodents, but it is consistent with the K-selected tendencies observed in afrotherian insectivores. Energetically, the basal metabolic demands of this species are well-documented. At the same ambient temperature of 33.6 °C, the maximum basal metabolic rate has been measured at 47.8 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 47.8 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at a temperature of 33.6 °C [T = 33.6 °C]. This relatively low metabolic expenditure is typical of insectivorous mammals that rely on a high-protein but often sporadic food supply.

Longevity data for Petrosaltator rozeti underscore its relatively slow-paced life history when considered alongside other small-bodied mammals. Under the stable conditions of captivity, with ambient temperature regulated at 33.6 °C [T = 33.6 °C], the maximum lifespan has been recorded to be approximately 7.2 years [am = approximately 7.2 years]. This figure is exceptional for an animal with an average adult body mass of around 63 grams, and it suggests a physiological resilience that allows for deferred senescence. In the wild, life expectancy is almost certainly shorter due to predation and environmental stochasticity, but the species’ capacity for extended longevity is linked to its low metabolic rate and the energetic trade-offs inherent in its reproductive strategy. The overall life-history syndrome of this North African elephant shrew thus blends rapid early maturation with a protracted adult lifespan, a combination that is particularly effective in the patchy and arid landscapes it inhabits.
